This will come.

It is counted as the ninth in the order of the revelation of the surahs; it was revealed after Surat al-A'la and before Surat al-Fajr.

Its number of verses is twenty.

* * *
It contains an explanation of the nobility of the believers and the virtues of their deeds, the censure of the polytheists and their faults, and the recompense of each.
And that God guides people to good, so He rewards those who are guided with the better of the two lives, and those who go astray with the opposite of that.

* * *

The opening of the speech with an oath follows the style of the two surahs before this one, and the purpose of that is what has been mentioned just above.

The connection between what is sworn by and what is sworn to is that people's striving has in it both good and evil, and these two resemble light and darkness; and people's striving issues forth in results, some beneficial and some harmful, just as the male and the female produce righteous and unrighteous offspring.

So it suited that state by an indication, representing it by the state of the night when the appearance of day follows it. This becomes clear in the answer to the oath in His words: (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾) up to His words: (﴿when it perishes﴾ [al-Layl: 11]).

Page 379

The object of (yaghsha) has been omitted to make the verb stand in the position of an intransitive one, because the lesson lies in its covering everything that its darkness covers.

Manifestation (tajalli) has been attributed to the day as praise for it, for the illumination that everyone sees and perceives, even those with sharp sight.

Tajalli means clarity, and the tajalli of the day is the clarity of its light; so it has the meaning of His words: (﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1]) and His words: (﴿By the morning brightness﴾ [al-Duha: 1]).

It is pointed out that the darkness of the night was dominant over the light of the day, and that the day follows it; and darkness is the original state of the inhabitants of the earth and of all the worlds bound to the solar system. Light came only after God created the sun. For this reason, reckoning of time began with nights, then days came to be used for reckoning.

Al-dhakar wa-al-untha (the male and the female): the two categories of kinds of animal. What is intended is specifically the creation of man and his formation from a male and a female, as He, the Exalted, said: (﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]), because he is the highest created being in the world of material things, and he is the one whose most subtle details the addressees can perceive, since it recurs in their own selves, males and females among them, unlike the procreation of animal offspring, for man perceives some of its states but does not count many of them.

The meaning: that wondrous creation, with the difference between the two states of maleness and femaleness while both emerge from one origin, and the procreation depending on their mating. So the oath is by an aspect of the divine attributes of action, which is a category of attributes whose establishment is not disputed; but the scholars of the principles of religion differed over whether attributes of action count among the attributes.

Page 380
Thus, according to al-Maturidi they are described as eternal, or they are regarded as an aspect of the attribute of power, in which case they are originated according to al-Ash'ari; and this reverts to a verbal disagreement.

The clause (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾) is the answer to the oath. The purpose of emphasizing with the oath is His words: (﴿and his wealth will not avail him when he perishes﴾ [al-Layl: 11]).

The essential meaning of sa'y (striving) is brisk, vigorous walking, and it is used here metaphorically for work and toil.

Shatta: the plural of shatit on the pattern fa'lá, like qatil and qatla, derived from al-shatt, which is intense dispersion; one says "shatta jam'uhum" when they scattered. What is meant here is diversity and difference in conditions, as in the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

Little complaining of the calamity that befalls him,
Much of desire, scattered in destinations and paths.
This is a metaphor or metonymy for the differing deeds, because dispersion entails difference.
The address in His words: (﴿Indeed, your efforts﴾) is to all people, believers and disbelievers alike.

Know that it has been narrated in the two Sahihs from 'Alqama, who said: "I entered, with a group of the companions of 'Abd Allah — meaning Ibn Mas'ud — Syria, and Abu al-Darda' heard of us, so he came to us and said: Which of you recites according to the recitation of 'Abd Allah? I said: I do. He said: How did you hear him recite (﴿By the night when it covers﴾)? I said: I heard him recite: (By the night when it covers, and the day when it appears, and the male and the female). He said: I bear witness that I heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it just like this." In al-Kashshaf it is called the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning it is established that he recited it thus. I have explained in the sixth introduction of this commentary the meaning of their saying: "the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ."

Likewise, he mentioned these views in al-Itqan, and he pointed out that this is due to what has been narrated as the occasion of revelation of the words of God Most High: (﴿As for him who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ [al-Layl: 5]), for it has been narrated that "it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari, regarding a palm tree from which orphans used to eat its dates, and it belonged to a man among the hypocrites, who prevented them from its fruit; so Abu al-Dahdah bought it in exchange for palm trees and made it theirs." This will come.

It is counted as the ninth in the order of the revelation of the surahs; it was revealed after Surat al-A'la and before Surat al-Fajr.

Its number of verses is twenty.

It contains an explanation of the nobility of the believers and the virtues of their deeds, the censure of the polytheists and their faults, and the recompense of each.
And that God guides people to good, so He rewards those who are guided with the better of the two lives, and those who go astray with the opposite of that.

And that He sent His Messenger ﷺ to remind [people] of God and what is with Him, so that whoever fears will benefit and will prosper.

And whoever was wretched turns away from the reminder, and his recompense will be the greatest fire. Those are the ones whom the love of what they are in, in this life, has prevented from taking heed.

(﴿By the night when it covers﴾) (﴿and by the day when it appears in splendor﴾) (﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾) (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾).
The opening of the speech with an oath follows the style of the two surahs before this one, and the purpose of that is what has been mentioned just above.

The connection between what is sworn by and what is sworn to is that people's striving has in it both good and evil, and these two resemble light and darkness; and people's striving issues forth in results, some beneficial and some harmful, just as the male and the female produce righteous and unrighteous offspring.

In the oath by the night and the day there is an alert to take lesson from them in inferring the wisdom of God's order in this universe and the wondrous nature of His power. The aspect of the night singled out for mention is the indication from its state of covering: it covers the side of the earth that it overspreads, and in it all existing things are enveloped by its darkness so that they do not appear to observers, because that is its strongest state. And from the states of the day, the state of its unveiling of existing things and its appearing over the earth in that manner is singled out for mention.

The explanation of covering and unveiling has already been given in the commentary on His words: (﴿By the day when it reveals it, and by the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 3-4]) in Surat al-Shams.

The oath by the night and the day was chosen for its suitability to the context, because the purpose of the surah is to explain the gulf between the state of the believers and the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter.

In this surah the mention of the night is begun, then the mention of the day, the reverse of what is in Surat al-Shams; because this surah was revealed some time before Surat al-Shams and it is the sixth of the surahs, and at that time disbelief was spread over people except a small group, and Islam had begun to become manifest. So it suited that state by an indication, representing it by the state of the night when the appearance of day follows it. This becomes clear in the answer to the oath in His words: (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾) up to His words: (﴿when it perishes﴾ [al-Layl: 11]).

Page 379
In His words: (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾) there is a general statement which conveys eagerness toward its detailed explanation in His words: (﴿As for him who gives﴾ [al-Layl: 5]) and what follows, so that its detail may settle in the mind.
The object of (yaghsha) has been omitted to make the verb stand in the position of an intransitive one, because the lesson lies in its covering everything that its darkness covers.

Manifestation (tajalli) has been attributed to the day as praise for it, for the illumination that everyone sees and perceives, even those with sharp sight.

Tajalli means clarity, and the tajalli of the day is the clarity of its light; so it has the meaning of His words: (﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1]) and His words: (﴿By the morning brightness﴾ [al-Duha: 1]).

It is pointed out that the darkness of the night was dominant over the light of the day, and that the day follows it; and darkness is the original state of the inhabitants of the earth and of all the worlds bound to the solar system. Light came only after God created the sun. For this reason, reckoning of time began with nights, then days came to be used for reckoning.

What is said about restricting the night with the adverbial clause, and restricting the day with a similar one, is like what is said regarding His words: (﴿By the day when it reveals it﴾ [al-Shams: 3]) and (﴿By the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 4]) in the preceding surah.

The "ma" in His words: (﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾) is verbal-masdariyya (a masdar-forming particle); God swears by one of the traces of His power, namely the creation of the two mates and what this requires of procreation.

Al-dhakar wa-al-untha (the male and the female): the two categories of kinds of animal. What is intended is specifically the creation of man and his formation from a male and a female, as He, the Exalted, said: (﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]), because he is the highest created being in the world of material things, and he is the one whose most subtle details the addressees can perceive, since it recurs in their own selves, males and females among them, unlike the procreation of animal offspring, for man perceives some of its states but does not count many of them.

The meaning: that wondrous creation, with the difference between the two states of maleness and femaleness while both emerge from one origin, and the procreation depending on their mating. So the oath is by an aspect of the divine attributes of action, which is a category of attributes whose establishment is not disputed; but the scholars of the principles of religion differed over whether attributes of action count among the attributes.

Page 380
Thus, according to al-Maturidi they are described as eternal, or they are regarded as an aspect of the attribute of power, in which case they are originated according to al-Ash'ari; and this reverts to a verbal disagreement.
In the surah of al-Shams the oath was by the proportioning of the soul, that is, the creation of reason and knowledge in man; but the oath here is by the creation of man's body and the difference of its two kinds. The clause (﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾) is the answer to the oath. The purpose of emphasizing with the oath is His words: (﴿and his wealth will not avail him when he perishes﴾ [al-Layl: 11]).

The essential meaning of sa'y (striving) is brisk, vigorous walking, and it is used here metaphorically for work and toil.

Shatta: the plural of shatit on the pattern fa'lá, like qatil and qatla, derived from al-shatt, which is intense dispersion; one says "shatta jam'uhum" when they scattered. What is meant here is diversity and difference in conditions, as in the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

Little complaining of the calamity that befalls him,
Much of desire, scattered in destinations and paths.
This is a metaphor or metonymy for the differing deeds, because dispersion entails difference.
The address in His words: (﴿Indeed, your efforts﴾) is to all people, believers and disbelievers alike.

Know that it has been narrated in the two Sahihs from 'Alqama, who said: "I entered, with a group of the companions of 'Abd Allah — meaning Ibn Mas'ud — Syria, and Abu al-Darda' heard of us, so he came to us and said: Which of you recites according to the recitation of 'Abd Allah? I said: I do. He said: How did you hear him recite (﴿By the night when it covers﴾)? I said: I heard him recite: (By the night when it covers, and the day when it appears, and the male and the female). He said: I bear witness that I heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it just like this." In al-Kashshaf it is called the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning it is established that he recited it thus. The interpretation of that is that he taught it to Abu al-Darda' at a time when the Qur'an was permitted to be recited with some variation; then that permission was abrogated (naskh) by what the Prophet ﷺ recited at the end of his life, which is what the readers of the Qur'an agreed upon and which was written in the mushaf in the time of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. I have explained in the sixth introduction of this commentary the meaning of their saying: "the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ."

[p. 381]

(﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah,﴾ ﴿and affirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿His wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾)

(Fa-amma) is a continuation and detailing of the general statement in His words, ﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾ [al-Layl 92:4]. The particle (amma) indicates both a condition and a detailing, and it implicitly contains a conditional particle and a conditional verb, since it means: "whatever may be the case." Detailing (tafsil) is the separation of a plurality whose members share a state but are distinguished from one another by a state that is worth clarifying. Its explanation has already been given at His words, ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾ [al-Fajr 89:15], in Surat al-Fajr.

What requires detailing here is the mentioned "effort," but the detailing was made by describing the strivers in His words, ﴿So as for he who gives﴾, because the important matter is the difference in the conditions of the strivers, and striving accompanies them. Thus, placing them in the detailing according to their efforts is equivalent to placing the efforts in the detailing. This is a variety (tafannun) of the eloquent forms of speech, from which two meanings result, like the words of al-Nabigha:

"I have been so afraid that my fear does not increase
beyond that of a wild goat on the cliff of al-Mataraj, alert."

That is: beyond the fear of a wild goat.

Among its examples is His words, ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:177], etc., in Surat al-Baqarah.

And His words, ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to [the deeds of] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day?﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:19], the verse, meaning: as the faith of one who believes in Allah.

The detailing of (shatta) is confined to two groups: a group made ready for ease and a group made ready for hardship, because these two states are the important ones in the context of urging toward good and warning against evil, and under them fall the various kinds of deeds, as in His words, ﴿That Day the people will depart in scattered groups to be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:6], ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:7], ﴿And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:8], in Surat al-Zalzalah.

It is also permissible that the detailing of (shatta) be understood as: those who give, fear Allah and affirm the best reward, and those who are miserly, consider themselves self-sufficient and deny the best reward. That is a number that can serve as an explanation of (shatta).

[p. 382]

The (man) in His words, ﴿Whoever gives﴾ etc., and His words, ﴿Whoever is miserly﴾ etc., includes everyone who performs giving, fears Allah and affirms the best reward. It is narrated that this was revealed because Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and freed him in order to save him from the torture of Umayya ibn Khalaf. Some exegetes mention Abu Sufyan ibn Harb instead of Umayya ibn Khalaf, and this is an error.

It has also been said that it was revealed concerning the case of Abu al-Dahdah with a hypocritical man, which will come. This latter view implies that the surah is Medinan, and the occasion of revelation does not restrict the generality of the verse.

The object of (a'ta, gave) is omitted, because the verb of giving, when intended to mean giving wealth without return, is treated as intransitive, due to the prevalence of its use for giving wealth; this is why wealth that is given as a gift is called (ata', gift). The intended meaning is the giving of zakat.

Likewise, the object of (ittaqa, feared) is omitted, because it is known that what is implied is: "feared Allah."

These three characteristics are among the characteristics of faith. So the meaning is: as for whoever was among the believers, as in His words, ﴿They said, "We were not among those who prayed,"﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:43] ﴿"And we did not used to feed the poor,"﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:44], meaning: we were not among the people of faith.

Likewise, the verb (bakhila, was miserly) has no mentioned complement, because what is intended by it is miserliness with wealth.

(Istaghna, considered himself self-sufficient) is made the counterpart of (ittaqa, feared). So what is meant by it is self-sufficiency from complying with the command of Allah and His call, because one who persists in disbelief and turns away from the call considers himself independent of Allah, content with the guardianship of the idols and his people. The sin and ta' in (istaghna) are for intensification of the verb, like the sin of (istajaba) in the sense of (ajaba, responded). It may also mean an increased seeking of wealth through miserliness with wealth, in which case the sin and ta' are for seeking. These characteristics are a metaphor (kinaya) for being one of the polytheists.

(Husna, best) is the feminine of (ahsan, best). Originally it is an adjective of an implied noun, and its feminine form indicates that the implied noun it modifies is regarded as feminine in form. It may refer to many things, such as reward, victory, a promise, or the final outcome.

This adjective may become a proper noun by prevalence. So it has been said: (al-husna) is Paradise; it has been said: the testimony of faith; it has been said: prayer; it has been said: zakat. In all these interpretations, affirming it means acknowledging that it will occur, and this is a metonymy (kinaya) for desire to attain it.

The sum of the possibilities revolves around affirming Allah's promise of what is good, whether reward, victory, or the replacement of what is lost. So this affirmation returns to faith.

It also implies that he performs the deeds through which he attains the best reward.

For this reason, in the other half, it is paired with His words, ﴿and denies the best reward﴾.

Easing (taysir) is making something easy to attain. The object of the verb of easing is the thing that is made easy, meaning not difficult, and the noun governed by the preposition (li) after it is the one for whose sake a difficult matter is made easy, and who benefits from the ease of the matter, as in His words, ﴿and ease my affair for me﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:26], and His words, ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar 54:17].

(Al-yusra, ease) in His words, (for ease) means that in which there is no hardship. Its feminine form is either by interpreting it as a state, meaning the state that does not burden him in the Hereafter, which is the state of bliss, or by interpreting it as a station. Al-yusra has been explained as Paradise, from Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujahid. The word may carry many meanings that fall within the meanings of what is beneficial and not burdensome to its possessor, i.e., what is suitable.

(Al-'usra, hardship) is either the state, namely the state of hardship and severity, or its station, namely Hell, because it is the place of hardship and severity for its people. Allah said, ﴿So that Day will be a difficult day﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:9], ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:10]. So the meaning of (nuyassiruhu, We shall ease him) is: We shall place him in the two courses of happiness and misery. Ibn 'Atiyyah explained it in this way. So the deeds of ease are the righteous ones, described as ease with regard to their outcome for their doer, and the deeds of hardship are the evil ones, described as hardship with regard to their outcome for their doer. Their feminine form is because each of them is an attribute of a category of deeds.

On this interpretation, the particle of future (sa-, will) is intended to indicate continuity from now until the end of life, as in His words, ﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾ [Yusuf 12:98].

The article (al-) in (al-yusra) and (al-'usra) is for generic definition or for specific reference, depending on the meanings.

[p. 384]

Since the arrangement of the structure in this verse has come contrary to what is immediately understood, in that the pronoun of the third person in (nuyassiruhu li-l-yusra), referring to (whoever gives and fears Allah), is made the one who is eased, and the pronoun of the third person in (nuyassiruhu li-l-'usra), referring to (whoever is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient), is made the one who is eased, meaning: the one for whom the difficult act becomes attainable; and since the two prepositional phrases (al-yusra) and (al-'usra) do not benefit from the ease of the one who gives or the one who is miserly, the structure of the verse must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: keeping the verb (nuyassiru, We shall ease) in its literal sense and making the speech operate contrary to the apparent requirement, through inversion (qalb), such that the original sentence would be: "We shall ease the ease for him, and We shall ease the hardship for him." There must be a motive for the inversion, and it is taken that the motive is to convey exaggeration in this easing, to the point that the one who is eased is made eased for, and the one eased for is made eased, in the manner in which they interpreted the Arabic saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

The second: that the easing is used as a metonymy (majaz mursal) for preparing and equipping, by the relation of necessity between preparing a thing for another thing and making it easy for it. In this case, the preposition (li-) in (li-l-yusra) and (li-l-'usra) is the preposition of causation, meaning: We shall ease him for the sake of ease or for the sake of hardship. So by ease is meant Paradise, and by hardship is meant Hell, on the basis that the two descriptions have become proper nouns by prevalence for Paradise and for Fire. Preparation is not for the pleasures of Paradise itself or the fire itself, so it is necessary to posit a genitive after the preposition that fits easing. It is therefore posited: "for entry into ease" and "for entry into hardship," meaning: We shall hasten that for him.

The meaning is: We shall make the entry of this one into Paradise swift and the entry of the other into the Fire swift, by likening it to what is made easy from difficulty, because the nature of the difficult is delay and the nature of the easy is speed. Allah said, ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf 50:44], meaning: swift and quick. On this interpretation, His words, ﴿So We shall ease him toward hardship﴾, become a metaphor of association (mushakalah) built upon a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyya), whose indicator is the word (al-'usra). What prompts this view is that the verb (nuyassiru) takes as its object the pronoun of those who (give, fear Allah, and affirm) and the pronoun of those who (are miserly, consider themselves self-sufficient, and deny). So it is an easing that arises from the occurrence of the deeds that the meaning of (ittaqa) or the meaning of (istaghna) comprises, so the deeds are necessarily prior. The easing comes after their occurrence, so it is

[p. 385]

the easing of what goes beyond their occurrence, meaning the easing of persistence in them and increase in them.

It is also possible that the meaning of the verse is: the easing is taken in its literal sense, and (al-yusra) is made an attribute, meaning the state of ease, and (al-'usra) meaning the state that is not ease. There is no inversion in the structure.

Easing in the sense of persistence in the deed is attested in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ali, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the cemetery of Baqi' al-Gharqad at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none of you but his seat in Paradise and his seat in the Fire has been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not then rely on that?' He said: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for the people of happiness, they are made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness, and as for the people of misery, they are made easy for the deeds of the people of misery.' Then he recited, ﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah, and affirms the best reward, We shall ease him toward ease. But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward, We shall ease him toward hardship.﴾" End of quotation.

The beginning of the hadith has no connection with what this verse includes. His words, "There is none of you but his seat has been written," etc., mean: Allah has known that a person will act by the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon them, or will act by the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon them. So His words "his seat has been written" make the writing a figure (tamthil) for Allah's knowledge of things, a knowledge that matches what will be, with no increase or decrease in it, like a written thing, which admits no addition or subtraction, unlike the spoken word, which is not written and so is not fixed.

From this arose the question of one who asked about the benefit of the deeds that people perform. The answer means: the benefit of righteous deeds is that they are a sign of a good outcome. Its opposite, evil deeds, is mentioned to complete the benefit, and it has no connection with the answer.

Its metaphor is not similar to what is used in this verse, because in the hadith the deeds of the people of happiness are the subject, so it is necessary that it be an easing of the deed, meaning preparing and equipping for deeds, whether righteous or evil.

What relates the verse to the prophetic words is that the Prophet (ﷺ) followed his speech by reciting ﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah﴾, etc., because he recited it as an explanation and as evidence for his speech. So the verse has a connection to the prophetic speech, and the place of argument is His words, ﴿We shall ease him﴾.

[p. 386]

Therefore the purpose of it is to establish that among the affairs of Allah the Exalted is an ease for the servant so that he acts by the deeds of happiness or the deeds of misery, whether his deed is a root of happiness, such as faith, or of misery, such as disbelief, or the deed is of the kind that increases happiness and decreases misery, and that is in proportion to the righteous deeds of one who is a believer. This is because the establishment of one of the two meanings of easing indicates the establishment of its genus, so it is suitable as evidence for the establishment of easing from its origin.

[p. 387]

Or the purpose of the verse's structure may be to furnish evidence for His saying, "Work" (i'malu). The verse mentions an action and mentions facilitation toward ease (al-yusra) and facilitation toward hardship (al-'usra). So the passage is a hint that action is the sign of facilitation. Here "ease" means happiness (al-sa'adah), and "hardship" means wretchedness (al-shaqawah). The referent of happiness is attaining Paradise, and the referent of wretchedness is plunging into the Fire.

Since the promise of facilitating ease is made to the one who has those attributes (al-silat), namely giving, piety, and affirming the best (al-husna), the use of the relative construction (al-mawsuliyyah, the relative-pronoun form) signals the basis for the predicate's structure, which is facilitation. It is therefore established that facilitation results from those attributes; that is, it is a recompense for performing them. Thus "the one who is facilitated" refers to being facilitated to persist in them. "Ease" is then an attribute of the actions. This is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar, using the explicit noun where a pronoun would be expected). The original would be "his actions are made easy for him" (mustaysir lahu a'maluhu). Instead of the pronoun, the attribute "ease" is used to praise those actions as made easy by God, as in His saying: ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ [al-A'la: 8] in Surah al-A'la.

The summary of the passage is that it explains the difference between God's knowledge of His servants' actions before they perform them and His address to them concerning His laws. What proceeds from people of outward and inward actions, up to the end of each person's life and his encounter with Him, is a sign for people of what God had already known. The two paths meet in the fact that action is the means of attaining Paradise or falling into Hell.

Giving is singled out for mention in His saying, ﴿As for him who gives and fears (God)﴾, even though "fears" (ittaqa) includes its meaning. Stinginess is singled out in His saying, ﴿But as for him who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾, even though "considers himself self-sufficient" (istaghna) includes it. This is to encourage the Muslims to give. Giving and piety are the emblem of the Muslims, along with affirming the best, while the opposite of these three is the emblem of the polytheists.

[p. 387 continues]

The verse contains the embellishment of combining with division (husn al-jam' ma'a al-taqsim) and the embellishment of antithesis (husn al-tibaq). There are four antitheses: between "gave" (a'ta) and "withheld" (bakhila), between "feared" (ittaqa) and "considered himself self-sufficient" (istaghna), between "affirmed" (saddaqa) and "denied" (kadhdhaba), and between "ease" (al-yusra) and "hardship" (al-'usra).

The clause ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿We will ease his way to hardship﴾. That is, "We will hasten him toward Hell." The implied sense is: "when he falls into it."

Taraddi means falling from a height to a lower place. The meaning is that the wealth he withheld will not avail him in the least against the punishment of the Fire.

The word "ma" (what) may be a negation, so the sense is: "and his wealth will certainly not avail him when he falls into Hell." It may also be interrogative, which is a question of denial and reproach, and on this reading the waw may be for resumption. The meaning would be: "And what will his wealth that he withheld avail him?"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that "a man among the hypocrites had a leaning palm tree in the house of a Muslim man who had dependents. Whenever a date fell from it, the children of that Muslim would eat it, and the owner of the palm would snatch the date from their hands. The Muslim complained of this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke to the owner of the palm, asking him to leave it for them, and he would have a palm in Paradise in return. But he did not do so. Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari heard of this, so he bought that palm from its owner in exchange for an orchard containing forty palms, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'O Messenger of God, take it from me in exchange for a palm in Paradise.' He (ﷺ) said, 'Yes, by the One in whose hand my soul is.' Then he gave it to the man who had the children."

'Ikrimah said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Then God the Exalted revealed ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1] up to His saying, 'toward hardship.'" This is a gharib (strange, weakly transmitted) report. Because of Ibn 'Abbas's statement, "Then God the Exalted revealed ﴿By the night when it covers﴾," a group said that the surah is Medinan. We have explained in the Fifth Introduction that it is very common in the speech of earlier scholars to say, "God revealed in such-and-such matter His saying such-and-such," and by this they mean that the incident is among the things that the verse encompasses.

[p. 388 continues]

It is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How many a heavy date-cluster in Paradise belongs to Abu al-Dahdah!" Bashshar ibn Burd alluded to it in his saying:

Indeed, the little palm, when desire inclines it,
is like a date-cluster that leaned over Abu al-Dahdah.

[p. 381]

(﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah,﴾ ﴿and affirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿His wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾)

(Fa-amma) is a continuation and detailing of the general statement in His words, ﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾ [al-Layl 92:4]. The particle (amma) indicates both a condition and a detailing, and it implicitly contains a conditional particle and a conditional verb, since it means: "whatever may be the case." Detailing (tafsil) is the separation of a plurality whose members share a state but are distinguished from one another by a state that is worth clarifying. Its explanation has already been given at His words, ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾ [al-Fajr 89:15], in Surat al-Fajr.

What requires detailing here is the mentioned "effort," but the detailing was made by describing the strivers in His words, ﴿So as for he who gives﴾, because the important matter is the difference in the conditions of the strivers, and striving accompanies them. Thus, placing them in the detailing according to their efforts is equivalent to placing the efforts in the detailing. The first: keeping the verb (nuyassiru, We shall ease) in its literal sense and making the speech operate contrary to the apparent requirement, through inversion (qalb), such that the original sentence would be: "We shall ease the ease for him, and We shall ease the hardship for him." There must be a motive for the inversion, and it is taken that the motive is to convey exaggeration in this easing, to the point that the one who is eased is made eased for, and the one eased for is made eased, in the manner in which they interpreted the Arabic saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

That is: beyond the fear of a wild goat.

The intended meaning is the giving of zakat.

Likewise, the object of (ittaqa, feared) is omitted, because it is known that what is implied is: "feared Allah."

These characteristics are a metaphor (kinaya) for being one of the polytheists.

This adjective may become a proper noun by prevalence. So it has been said: (al-husna) is Paradise; it has been said: the testimony of faith; it has been said: prayer; it has been said: zakat. In all these interpretations, affirming it means acknowledging that it will occur, and this is a metonymy (kinaya) for desire to attain it.

The sum of the possibilities revolves around affirming Allah's promise of what is good, whether reward, victory, or the replacement of what is lost. So this affirmation returns to faith.

It also implies that he performs the deeds through which he attains the best reward.

For this reason, in the other half, it is paired with His words, ﴿and denies the best reward﴾.

Al-yusra has been explained as Paradise, from Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujahid. The first: keeping the verb (nuyassiru, We shall ease) in its literal sense and making the speech operate contrary to the apparent requirement, through inversion (qalb), such that the original sentence would be: "We shall ease the ease for him, and We shall ease the hardship for him." There must be a motive for the inversion, and it is taken that the motive is to convey exaggeration in this easing, to the point that the one who is eased is made eased for, and the one eased for is made eased, in the manner in which they interpreted the Arabic saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

The second: that the easing is used as a metonymy (majaz mursal) for preparing and equipping, by the relation of necessity between preparing a thing for another thing and making it easy for it. So by ease is meant Paradise, and by hardship is meant Hell, on the basis that the two descriptions have become proper nouns by prevalence for Paradise and for Fire. It is therefore posited: "for entry into ease" and "for entry into hardship," meaning: We shall hasten that for him.

The meaning is: We shall make the entry of this one into Paradise swift and the entry of the other into the Fire swift, by likening it to what is made easy from difficulty, because the nature of the difficult is delay and the nature of the easy is speed. The first: keeping the verb (nuyassiru, We shall ease) in its literal sense and making the speech operate contrary to the apparent requirement, through inversion (qalb), such that the original sentence would be: "We shall ease the ease for him, and We shall ease the hardship for him." There must be a motive for the inversion, and it is taken that the motive is to convey exaggeration in this easing, to the point that the one who is eased is made eased for, and the one eased for is made eased, in the manner in which they interpreted the Arabic saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

As for the people of happiness, they are made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness, and as for the people of misery, they are made easy for the deeds of the people of misery.' Then he recited, ﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah, and affirms the best reward, We shall ease him toward ease. But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward, We shall ease him toward hardship.﴾" End of quotation.

The beginning of the hadith has no connection with what this verse includes. His words, "There is none of you but his seat has been written," etc., mean: Allah has known that a person will act by the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon them, or will act by the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon them. So His words "his seat has been written" make the writing a figure (tamthil) for Allah's knowledge of things, a knowledge that matches what will be, with no increase or decrease in it, like a written thing, which admits no addition or subtraction, unlike the spoken word, which is not written and so is not fixed.

From this arose the question of one who asked about the benefit of the deeds that people perform. The answer means: the benefit of righteous deeds is that they are a sign of a good outcome. Its opposite, evil deeds, is mentioned to complete the benefit, and it has no connection with the answer.

Its metaphor is not similar to what is used in this verse, because in the hadith the deeds of the people of happiness are the subject, so it is necessary that it be an easing of the deed, meaning preparing and equipping for deeds, whether righteous or evil.

What relates the verse to the prophetic words is that the Prophet (ﷺ) followed his speech by reciting ﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah﴾, etc., because he recited it as an explanation and as evidence for his speech. So the verse has a connection to the prophetic speech, and the place of argument is His words, ﴿We shall ease him﴾.

Therefore the purpose of it is to establish that among the affairs of Allah the Exalted is an ease for the servant so that he acts by the deeds of happiness or the deeds of misery, whether his deed is a root of happiness, such as faith, or of misery, such as disbelief, or the deed is of the kind that increases happiness and decreases misery, and that is in proportion to the righteous deeds of one who is a believer. This is because the establishment of one of the two meanings of easing indicates the establishment of its genus, so it is suitable as evidence for the establishment of easing from its origin.

Or the purpose of the verse's structure may be to furnish evidence for His saying, "Work" (i'malu). The verse mentions an action and mentions facilitation toward ease (al-yusra) and facilitation toward hardship (al-'usra). So the passage is a hint that action is the sign of facilitation. Here "ease" means happiness (al-sa'adah), and "hardship" means wretchedness (al-shaqawah). The referent of happiness is attaining Paradise, and the referent of wretchedness is plunging into the Fire.

Since the promise of facilitating ease is made to the one who has those attributes (al-silat), namely giving, piety, and affirming the best (al-husna), the use of the relative construction (al-mawsuliyyah, the relative-pronoun form) signals the basis for the predicate's structure, which is facilitation. It is therefore established that facilitation results from those attributes; that is, it is a recompense for performing them. Thus "the one who is facilitated" refers to being facilitated to persist in them. "Ease" is then an attribute of the actions. This is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar, using the explicit noun where a pronoun would be expected). The original would be "his actions are made easy for him" (mustaysir lahu a'maluhu). Instead of the pronoun, the attribute "ease" is used to praise those actions as made easy by God, as in His saying: ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ [al-A'la: 8] in Surah al-A'la.

The summary of the passage is that it explains the difference between God's knowledge of His servants' actions before they perform them and His address to them concerning His laws. What proceeds from people of outward and inward actions, up to the end of each person's life and his encounter with Him, is a sign for people of what God had already known. The two paths meet in the fact that action is the means of attaining Paradise or falling into Hell.

Giving is singled out for mention in His saying, ﴿As for him who gives and fears (God)﴾, even though "fears" (ittaqa) includes its meaning. Stinginess is singled out in His saying, ﴿But as for him who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾, even though "considers himself self-sufficient" (istaghna) includes it. This is to encourage the Muslims to give. Giving and piety are the emblem of the Muslims, along with affirming the best, while the opposite of these three is the emblem of the polytheists.

The verse contains the embellishment of combining with division (husn al-jam' ma'a al-taqsim) and the embellishment of antithesis (husn al-tibaq). There are four antitheses: between "gave" (a'ta) and "withheld" (bakhila), between "feared" (ittaqa) and "considered himself self-sufficient" (istaghna), between "affirmed" (saddaqa) and "denied" (kadhdhaba), and between "ease" (al-yusra) and "hardship" (al-'usra).

Taraddi means falling from a height to a lower place. The meaning is that the wealth he withheld will not avail him in the least against the punishment of the Fire.

The word "ma" (what) may be a negation, so the sense is: "and his wealth will certainly not avail him when he falls into Hell." It may also be interrogative, which is a question of denial and reproach, and on this reading the waw may be for resumption. The meaning would be: "And what will his wealth that he withheld avail him?"

(﴿So as for he who gives and fears Allah,﴾ ﴿and affirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We shall ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿His wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾)

Detailing (tafsil) is the separation of a plurality whose members share a state but are distinguished from one another by a state that is worth clarifying. Its explanation has already been given at His words, ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾ [al-Fajr 89:15], in Surat al-Fajr.

What requires detailing here is the mentioned "effort," but the detailing was made by describing the strivers in His words, ﴿So as for he who gives﴾, because the important matter is the difference in the conditions of the strivers, and striving accompanies them. Thus, placing them in the detailing according to their efforts is equivalent to placing the efforts in the detailing. This is a variety (tafannun) of the eloquent forms of speech, from which two meanings result, like the words of al-Nabigha:

"I have been so afraid that my fear does not increase
beyond that of a wild goat on the cliff of al-Mataraj, alert."

That is: beyond the fear of a wild goat.

Among its examples is His words, ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:177], etc., in Surat al-Baqarah.

It is also permissible that the detailing of (shatta) be understood as: those who give, fear Allah and affirm the best reward, and those who are miserly, consider themselves self-sufficient and deny the best reward. That is a number that can serve as an explanation of (shatta).

[p. 382]

The (man) in His words, ﴿Whoever gives﴾ etc., and His words, ﴿Whoever is miserly﴾ etc., includes everyone who performs giving, fears Allah and affirms the best reward. It is narrated that this was revealed because Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf and freed him in order to save him from the torture of Umayya ibn Khalaf. Some exegetes mention Abu Sufyan ibn Harb instead of Umayya ibn Khalaf, and this is an error.

It has also been said that it was revealed concerning the case of Abu al-Dahdah with a hypocritical man, which will come. This latter view implies that the surah is Medinan, and the occasion of revelation does not restrict the generality of the verse.

The object of (a'ta, gave) is omitted, because the verb of giving, when intended to mean giving wealth without return, is treated as intransitive, due to the prevalence of its use for giving wealth; this is why wealth that is given as a gift is called (ata', gift). The intended meaning is the giving of zakat.

Likewise, the object of (ittaqa, feared) is omitted, because it is known that what is implied is: "feared Allah."

These three characteristics are among the characteristics of faith. So the meaning is: as for whoever was among the believers, as in His words, ﴿They said, "We were not among those who prayed,"﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:43] ﴿"And we did not used to feed the poor,"﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:44], meaning: we were not among the people of faith.

Likewise, the verb (bakhila, was miserly) has no mentioned complement, because what is intended by it is miserliness with wealth.

(Istaghna, considered himself self-sufficient) is made the counterpart of (ittaqa, feared). So what is meant by it is self-sufficiency from complying with the command of Allah and His call, because one who persists in disbelief and turns away from the call considers himself independent of Allah, content with the guardianship of the idols and his people. The sin and ta' in (istaghna) are for intensification of the verb, like the sin of (istajaba) in the sense of (ajaba, responded). It may also mean an increased seeking of wealth through miserliness with wealth, in which case the sin and ta' are for seeking. These characteristics are a metaphor (kinaya) for being one of the polytheists.

(Husna, best) is the feminine of (ahsan, best). Originally it is an adjective of an implied noun, and its feminine form indicates that the implied noun it modifies is regarded as feminine in form. It may refer to many things, such as reward, victory, a promise, or the final outcome.

This adjective may become a proper noun by prevalence. So it has been said: (al-husna) is Paradise; it has been said: the testimony of faith; it has been said: prayer; it has been said: zakat. In all these interpretations, affirming it means acknowledging that it will occur, and this is a metonymy (kinaya) for desire to attain it.

The sum of the possibilities revolves around affirming Allah's promise of what is good, whether reward, victory, or the replacement of what is lost. So this affirmation returns to faith.

It also implies that he performs the deeds through which he attains the best reward.

For this reason, in the other half, it is paired with His words, ﴿and denies the best reward﴾.

Easing (taysir) is making something easy to attain. The object of the verb of easing is the thing that is made easy, meaning not difficult, and the noun governed by the preposition (li) after it is the one for whose sake a difficult matter is made easy, and who benefits from the ease of the matter, as in His words, ﴿and ease my affair for me﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:26], and His words, ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar 54:17].

(Al-yusra, ease) in His words, (for ease) means that in which there is no hardship. Its feminine form is either by interpreting it as a state, meaning the state that does not burden him in the Hereafter, which is the state of bliss, or by interpreting it as a station. Al-yusra has been explained as Paradise, from Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujahid. The word may carry many meanings that fall within the meanings of what is beneficial and not burdensome to its possessor, i.e., what is suitable.

(Al-'usra, hardship) is either the state, namely the state of hardship and severity, or its station, namely Hell, because it is the place of hardship and severity for its people. Allah said, ﴿So that Day will be a difficult day﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:9], ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:10]. So the deeds of ease are the righteous ones, described as ease with regard to their outcome for their doer, and the deeds of hardship are the evil ones, described as hardship with regard to their outcome for their doer. Their feminine form is because each of them is an attribute of a category of deeds.

On this interpretation, the particle of future (sa-, will) is intended to indicate continuity from now until the end of life, as in His words, ﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾ [Yusuf 12:98].

The article (al-) in (al-yusra) and (al-'usra) is for generic definition or for specific reference, depending on the meanings.

Since the arrangement of the structure in this verse has come contrary to what is immediately understood, in that the pronoun of the third person in (nuyassiruhu li-l-yusra), referring to (whoever gives and fears Allah), is made the one who is eased, and the pronoun of the third person in (nuyassiruhu li-l-'usra), referring to (whoever is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient), is made the one who is eased, meaning: the one for whom the difficult act becomes attainable; and since the two prepositional phrases (al-yusra) and (al-'usra) do not benefit from the ease of the one who gives or the one who is miserly, the structure of the verse must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: keeping the verb (nuyassiru, We shall ease) in its literal sense and making the speech operate contrary to the apparent requirement, through inversion (qalb), such that the original sentence would be: "We shall ease the ease for him, and We shall ease the hardship for him." There must be a motive for the inversion, and it is taken that the motive is to convey exaggeration in this easing, to the point that the one who is eased is made eased for, and the one eased for is made eased, in the manner in which they interpreted the Arabic saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

The second: that the easing is used as a metonymy (majaz mursal) for preparing and equipping, by the relation of necessity between preparing a thing for another thing and making it easy for it. In this case, the preposition (li-) in (li-l-yusra) and (li-l-'usra) is the preposition of causation, meaning: We shall ease him for the sake of ease or for the sake of hardship. So by ease is meant Paradise, and by hardship is meant Hell, on the basis that the two descriptions have become proper nouns by prevalence for Paradise and for Fire. Preparation is not for the pleasures of Paradise itself or the fire itself, so it is necessary to posit a genitive after the preposition that fits easing. It is therefore posited: "for entry into ease" and "for entry into hardship," meaning: We shall hasten that for him.

The meaning is: We shall make the entry of this one into Paradise swift and the entry of the other into the Fire swift, by likening it to what is made easy from difficulty, because the nature of the difficult is delay and the nature of the easy is speed. Allah said, ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf 50:44], meaning: swift and quick. What prompts this view is that the verb (nuyassiru) takes as its object the pronoun of those who (give, fear Allah, and affirm) and the pronoun of those who (are miserly, consider themselves self-sufficient, and deny). So it is an easing that arises from the occurrence of the deeds that the meaning of (ittaqa) or the meaning of (istaghna) comprises, so the deeds are necessarily prior. The easing comes after their occurrence, so it is

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 92, verses 12–13:

﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the content of the preceding discourse, from His saying: (﴿But as for him who gives﴾ [al-Layl: 5]) up to His saying: (for the difficult). This is for the purpose of placing the responsibility on the one who has come to the difficult path, since God has given him an excuse by guiding him through the call of Islam to goodness, yet he turned away from being guided by his own choice and acquired evil deeds. Facilitation toward ease comes about when the servant inclines toward performing good deeds, and facilitation toward difficulty comes about when he inclines toward performing evil deeds. That inclination is what al-Ash'ari called acquisition (kasb), while the Mu'tazila named it the servant's power (qudrat al-'abd), and it is also what the Jabriyya confused and named compulsion (jabr).

The emphasis of the statement with (inna) and the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtida') suggests that this is a response to what stirs in the souls of the people of misguidance upon hearing the preceding warning, namely their denial that, had God willed, He would have compelled them to faith rather than calling them to it. It is related of them in another verse: (﴿And they said, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20]).

The particle (ʿalā, upon) when it falls between a noun and what indicates a verb conveys the meaning of obligation, i.e., "guidance of the people is incumbent upon Us." The attachment of a collective noun to a pronoun does not indicate generality, so the verse does not indicate that he gave all of his wealth.

The lam (اللّامُ) is the lam of initiation, for emphasizing the predicate.

This is one of the comprehensive expressions (مِن جَوامِعِ الكَلِمِ), for everything that those who desire good desire falls under it. With this surah the medium surahs of the Mufassal (وسَطِ المُفَصَّلِ) end.

The fa' (فاء) may be a mere sequential particle of mention (لِمُجَرَّدِ التَّفْرِيعِ الذِّكْرِيِّ), if the verb (أنْذَرْتُكم) is used in its literal past sense and the intended warning is that comprised in His saying: ﴿As for he who withholds and considers himself free of need, and denies the best, We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 8–10], up to His saying, ﴿will perish﴾ [al-Layl: 11]. This fa' is similar in meaning to the eloquent fa' (فاء الفصيحة), because it indicates regard for the content of the speech that precedes it, namely the sequencing of a detailed warning upon a general warning.

The fa' may also be a sequential particle of meaning (لِلتَّفْرِيعِ المَعْنَوِيِّ), so that the verb (﴿anzartukum﴾ [Fussilat: 13]) is intended in the present sense. It was phrased in the past tense to bring the time of the past close to the present, as in: "The prayer has been established" (قَدْ قامَتِ الصَّلاةُ), and the saying: "I insist upon you to do such-and-such" (عَزَمْتُ عَلَيْكَ إلّا ما فَعَلْتَ كَذا), meaning: "I insist" (أعْزِمُ). It is also like the phrasing of contracts: "I have sold" (بِعْتُ). It is a sequence upon the statement ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12], and the meaning is: "Our guidance [to you]; so I have warned you," for the sake of conveying guidance fully.

The indefiniteness of (نارًا) is for the sake of awe, and the clause (تَلَظّى) is a qualifier. (تَلَظّى) means: it blazes intensely due to the severity of its kindling. It is derived from al-laẓā (اللَّظى), the verbal noun of: "the fire blazed" (لَظِيَتِ النّارُ), on the pattern of "was pleased" (رَضِيَتْ), when it flared up. The original form of (تَلَظّى) is (تَتَلَظّى) with two tā's, one of which was dropped for brevity.

The clause (﴿None will enter it except the most wretched﴾) is a second qualifier, or a circumstantial clause, relating to (نارًا) after it has been described. This is a specific Fire, prepared for the disbelievers, and it is the one referred to in His saying: ﴿Fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. The indication of this is His saying: ﴿and the most righteous will be kept far from it﴾, and so on.

Al-Qurtubi mentions that Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: "This is the verse on account of which the People of Irja' (أهْلُ الإرْجاءِ) argued for irja'. They claimed that none enters the Fire except a disbeliever. The matter is not as they supposed: this is a Fire described by a specific description; none burns in this Fire except the one who denied and turned away. The people of the Fire have grades, and among them the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire." End of quotation.

The meaning is: "None will enter it except you."

The word (الأشْقى) is followed by the description (﴿the one who denied and turned away﴾) to add emphasis that they are the ones intended, for they know that they denied the Messenger (ﷺ) and turned away, that is, they turned aside from the Qur'an. This description was confined to them at that time, for in the era of the rise of Islam people were of two groups: either a disbeliever, or a believing God-fearing person. Those who had embraced Islam did not commit grave sins, for they had devoted themselves wholeheartedly to Islam. For this reason (﴿and the most righteous will be kept far from it﴾) is connected to it, in explicit statement of the implied meaning of restriction, and to complete the contrast.

(الأشْقى) and (الأتْقى) are intended to mean: the one of great wretchedness, and the one of great piety. Similar usage is common in speech.

Al-Qurtubi also mentions that Malik said: "'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz led us in prayer and recited ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1]. When he reached ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾, weeping overcame him, and he could not continue because of his weeping. So he left it and recited another surah."

The description of (الأشْقى) by the relative clause (﴿the one who denied and turned away﴾) and the description of (الأتْقى) by the relative clause (﴿the one who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾) indicate that the relative clause has a causal role in the ruling.

Between (الأشْقى) and (الأتْقى) there is the embellishment of jinās mudāri' (الجِناسِ المُضارِعِ), a near-paronomasia.

The clause (يَتَزَكّى) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (يُؤْتِي). The purpose of this circumstantial clause is to alert that he gives his wealth with the aim of gain and of increase in reward, as an implicit reproach to the polytheists who give wealth for boasting, for showing off, and for corruption and immorality.

(التَّزَكِّي) means: to exert effort to attain growth (تَكَلُّفُ الزَّكاءِ), and (الزَّكاء) is growth in goodness.

(المالُ) is a collective noun (اسْمُ جِنْسٍ) for what a person owns of things he benefits from either in their substance or in their yield and produce, such as livestock, lands, private wells, and trees owned by their possessors.

Among some Arabs, like the people of Yathrib, it is used for palm trees.

The attachment of a collective noun to a pronoun does not indicate generality, so the verse does not indicate that he gave all of his wealth.

As for His saying: ﴿and no one has a favor upon him to be repaid﴾, the commentators agree that the first person intended by this relative clause is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ), when he freed Bilal. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr did not do that except because of a favor Bilal had done for him." This is a statement of their slander, by which they justified to themselves their dislike that Abu Bakr had done it out of love for the Muslims. So God revealed His refutation of them through His saying: ﴿and no one has a favor upon him to be repaid﴾, intending by it some of those covered by the generality of ﴿the one who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾. This resembles mentioning a particular instance of a general term, and it does not specify the generality. However, since this situation was not common among the causes of giving wealth, it became clear that what is intended is a specific known circumstance, unlike His saying: ﴿and gives wealth, despite loving it, to relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God. We desire no reward from you, nor thanks﴾ [al-Insan: 9].

(عِنْدَهُ) is a locative adverb, and it is used here metaphorically to mean that the favor is firmly lodged in the one to whom it is attributed, as a thing present in a near place. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Who for us has, in its favor, signs three, in all of which there is decision?"

(مِن نِعْمَةٍ) is the subject of (ما), the negation particle, and it is governed by the redundant (مِن), which is added in negation to strengthen the negation. The exception in (﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾) is discontinuous (مُنْقَطِعٌ), meaning: "But rather, seeking the countenance of God."

(الِابْتِغاءُ) is seeking with diligence, for it is more emphatic than (البَغْيِ).

(الوَجْهُ) is used with the meaning of the essence, as in His saying: ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27]. The meaning of seeking the essence is seeking the good pleasure of God.

His saying: ﴿and he is going to be well pleased﴾ is a promise of abundant reward that will please its recipient. This completes His saying: ﴿and the most righteous will be kept far from it﴾, because that only indicated that he is saved from the torment of the Fire. The context requires limiting it to that for the purpose of contrast with His saying: ﴿None will enter it except the most wretched﴾, so it is completed here by mentioning what has been prepared for him of good things.

The particle (سَوْفَ) is for certainty of the promise in the future, as in His saying: ﴿He said: I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ [Yusuf: 98]. That is, His good pleasure will permeate the extended future.

The lam (اللّامُ) is the lam of initiation, for emphasizing the predicate.

This is one of the comprehensive expressions (مِن جَوامِعِ الكَلِمِ), for everything that those who desire good desire falls under it. With this surah the medium surahs of the Mufassal (وسَطِ المُفَصَّلِ) end.
